paragraph: “PHILIP THE EVANGELIST, WHICH WAS ONE OF THE SEVEN” (ACTS 21:8) · CALLED IN ACTS 6

blocks.text: “PHILIP THE EVANGELIST, WHICH WAS ONE OF THE SEVEN” (ACTS 21:8) · CALLED IN ACTS 6
Philip the evangelist. Preached in Samaria, baptized an Ethiopian official on the Gaza road, and settled at Caesarea.
ALSO CALLED
Philip, one of the Seven
FROM
When Paul passed through, years after Acts 8, Philip had a house at Caesarea, where Paul's company stayed “many days”.
TRADE
Scripture does not say
FAMILY
“The same man had four daughters, virgins, which did prophesy.”
WRITINGS
None
BACKGROUND
Home, trade and family
FROM
FAMILY
“The same man had four daughters, virgins, which did prophesy.” Acts 21:9
From the textScripture names no wife, parents or home town, and does not give the daughters' names. Acts 21:8–9
THE CALLING
Called, as 2 accounts tell it
“they chose Stephen, a man full of faith and of the Holy Ghost, and Philip”
Acts 6:5 (KJV) →
WHERE HE WENT
Acts and after
Dashed pins are places known only from later tradition, not from Scripture.
Jerusalem · Chosen as one of the Seven. Acts 6:5–6
Samaria · “The city of Samaria” where he preached (Acts 8:5). Acts 8:5 Acts 8:14
Gaza (the desert road toward it) · He was sent to the road from Jerusalem “unto Gaza, which is desert”; the meeting place on the road is not named. Acts 8:26
Ethiopia · Home of the official he baptized. Acts 8:27
Azotus (Ashdod) · Where he was “found” after the baptism. Acts 8:40
Caesarea · His home when Paul visited. Acts 8:40 Acts 21:8
Hierapolis (in tradition) · tradition · Polycrates and Proclus (about 190-200) place a Philip and his daughters here; which Philip is disputed.
IN ACTS AND THE LETTERS
In Samaria the people heard him and saw the miracles: unclean spirits came out, the palsied and lame were healed, “and there was great joy in that city”. Acts 8:6–8
Men and women believed and were baptized; Simon, who had used sorcery there, also believed, was baptized and “continued with Philip”. Acts 8:9–13
The apostles at Jerusalem sent Peter and John, who prayed for the Samaritans to receive the Holy Ghost; Simon then offered them money. Acts 8:14–24

An angel sent him toward the desert road from Jerusalem to Gaza. There he met an Ethiopian eunuch, treasurer of Candace queen of the Ethiopians, reading Isaiah in his chariot; Philip “began at the same scripture, and preached unto him Jesus”. Acts 8:26–35
At a water the eunuch asked, “what doth hinder me to be baptized?” Philip baptized him; the Spirit “caught away Philip”, and the eunuch went on his way rejoicing. Acts 8:36–39

From the textActs 8:37 (Philip's “If thou believest with all thine heart, thou mayest” and the eunuch's confession) is in the Greek text the KJV translated; Tischendorf's Greek and the Revised Version (1881) leave it out. Acts 8:37
He was “found at Azotus”, and preached in all the cities until he came to Caesarea. Acts 8:40
Paul's company stayed in his house at Caesarea; there the prophet Agabus foretold Paul's binding at Jerusalem. Acts 21:8–11
From the textThe last verse that names him is Acts 21:8. Scripture does not record his death. Acts 21:8
COMPANIONS
Who was with him
Each line joins him to someone Scripture places beside him.
Stephen Chosen with him as one of the Seven. Acts 6:5
Peter Sent with John by the apostles to Samaria after Philip's preaching there. Acts 8:14–17
John son of Zebedee Sent with Peter to Samaria after Philip's preaching there. Acts 8:14–17
Simon the sorcerer Believed, was baptized and “continued with Philip”. Acts 8:13
The Ethiopian official “An eunuch of great authority under Candace”, whom Philip taught from Isaiah and baptized. Acts 8:27–38
Paul Stayed many days in his house at Caesarea on the way to Jerusalem. Acts 21:8–10
Agabus Came to Philip's house and foretold Paul's arrest. Acts 21:10–11
HOW THE STORY ENDS
Scripture says, tradition says
SCRIPTURE SAYS
From the textScripture last shows him at home in Caesarea with his four daughters (Acts 21:8-9) and records nothing of his death. Acts 21:8–9
TRADITION SAYS

“Philip, one of the twelve apostles, who sleeps in Hierapolis, and his two aged virgin daughters, and another daughter who lived in the Holy Spirit and now rests at Ephesus.”[1] Who says so: Polycrates of Ephesus, letter to Victor of Rome, quoted by Eusebius, Church History 3.31.3, about AD 190

“There were four prophetesses, the daughters of Philip, at Hierapolis in Asia. Their tomb is there and the tomb of their father.”[1] Who says so: Proclus, in the Dialogue of Gaius, quoted by Eusebius, Church History 3.31.4, about AD 200

Papias “heard a wonderful tale from the daughters of Philip”: that “in his time” (Philip's, McGiffert explains) one rose from the dead. Eusebius calls this Philip “the apostle”.[1] Who says so: Papias, as reported by Eusebius, Church History 3.39.9, Papias early 2nd century; Eusebius about 325
At Caesarea the pilgrim Paula was shown “the humble abode of Philip; and the chambers of his daughters the four virgins”.[4] Who says so: Jerome, Letter 108.8 (to Eustochium), written AD 404

Another tradition makes Philip the first bishop of Tralles in Asia, with his daughters living there. Hunter (ISBE, 1915) reports it; its earliest source has not been identified here.[20] Who says so: Reported by Hunter (ISBE, 1915), earliest source not identified
OPEN QUESTIONS
Where readers have differed
The apostle, one of the Twelve

Polycrates of Ephesus (about AD 190); J. B. Lightfoot (commentary on Colossians, 1875), as reported by McGiffert; C. M. Kerr (ISBE, 1915, “Philip”), for whom “The evidence seems conclusive” that the apostle's last years were spent in Phrygia
Polycrates calls him “one of the twelve apostles”. Lightfoot held that Polycrates was right and that the apostle, not the evangelist, was buried there.[1][2][27]
The evangelist, with his prophesying daughters
Proclus (about 200), whose description matches Acts; A. C. McGiffert (1890)

Acts gives the evangelist “four daughters, virgins, which did prophesy”, and Proclus speaks of “four prophetesses, the daughters of Philip” at Hierapolis. McGiffert thinks later generations would naturally fold the evangelist into the apostle of the same name. Acts 21:8–9 [1][2]
One man: the two are the same Philip
Eusebius (about 325), who quotes Polycrates on the apostle and Acts 21:8-9 on the evangelist side by side
Eusebius sets the two reports together without comment, as if of one man; McGiffert notes that Eusebius took the apostle and the evangelist to be identical. Acts 21:8–9 [1][2]
IN SCRIPTURE
Every passage
CHAPTERS · 3
Acts 6 Acts 8 Acts 21
PASSAGES · 3
Acts 6:1–6 Acts 8:1–40 Acts 21:7–15
WHAT SCRIPTURE DOES NOT SAY
Scripture does not say where Philip came from, how he came to believe, or why he is called “the evangelist”.
Scripture does not name his daughters, say what their prophesying was, or tell what became of the family after Acts 21.
Scripture does not tell how or where he died.
IDENTIFICATIONS THIS PAGE RELIES ON

From the textThis is not Philip the apostle, one of the Twelve (Matthew 10:3; John 1:43). Luke keeps them apart: the Seven were chosen so that the Twelve could keep to prayer and the word (Acts 6:2-5), and Acts 21:8 calls this man “one of the seven”. Matthew 10:3 John 1:43 Acts 6:2–5 Acts 21:8

From the textThe Philip who preached in Samaria and baptized the Ethiopian (Acts 8) is taken to be this Philip: all but the apostles had been scattered (Acts 8:1), the apostles at Jerusalem sent Peter and John to his converts (8:14), and Acts leaves him at Caesarea (8:40), where Philip the evangelist lives in Acts 21:8. Acts 8:1 Acts 8:5 Acts 8:14 Acts 8:40 Acts 21:8

Early church · Eusebius (trans. A. C. McGiffert, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, series 2, vol. 1), 1890Early writers confused the two Philips. Polycrates (about AD 190) speaks of “Philip, one of the twelve apostles, who sleeps in Hierapolis” with his daughters; Eusebius (about 325) quotes him and then quotes Acts 21:8-9 about the evangelist's daughters as if of the same man. Acts 21:8–9 [1][2]

Scholars' viewMcGiffert (1890) judges that “Philip the apostle and Philip the evangelist are here confounded”, and notes that Eusebius treats them as one man. Hunter (ISBE, 1915) also writes that in the Hierapolis tradition “in all probability the evangelist is confounded with the apostle”.[2][20]
